Legit command line hacking makes this game both more fun and more frustrating (for some). You can use the mouse to click on things, but to get there you have to use command line entries first, which requires you to remember them as you go along and that, for me at least, can be difficult. But a simple pen and paper can overcome that.

That being said, is it still fun? To me, hell yes. 
It brings me back to my first days of computing using Basic on a C64 and then a DOS machine. 
On top of that the soundtrack is subtle, but well within the tone of the game and never overshadows anything.

I recommend this to anyone who wants a more realistic, but not over the top, hacking game.

Hacknet is not "an immersive, terminal-based hacking simulator for PC", this here is just a lie and I actually would say may be a detriment to the game depending on who you are and how you take those words.

If you're like me and you essentially expected a hacking simulator where you did as you please, hacked who you wanted to hack, and cause mayhem or the like, this is not what this game is about. You're better off looking at Uplink and getting UplinkOS.

What you're really getting from Hacknet is actually a sort of immersive novel, but you're a silent protagonist who probably button mashes the keyboard when sending e-mails.

Hacknet is very much the story about a recently deceased hacker named Bit. It's very much about trying to uncover what it was that Bit was doing that got him killed.

Hacknet is not a game you are going to be spending nearly 20 hours of your life playing though. At the moment of writing, I have 17, but that mostly comes from me picking the game back up again in previous attempts to play the game, and realizing that I have no idea what I'm doing at all, and starting back from the beginning to figure out what things did what.

The reality is, this game is actually about 8 hours or so in length, maybe a couple more if you get a tad lost. It's sort of hard to say, I would also wager it could be 10.

[b]But a thumbs up though, why?[/b] Well that's simply because this game does something interesting in all of this, and that is create interesting setups here and there for you to complete. Be it in one instance hacking into a fictional fast food chicken restaurants servers to find their secret recipe, death row records, [i]hospital equipment[/i], or deleting the save file of a user from a clicker game, Hacknet tries to give you interesting jobs in what would become a tedious routine for some.

If you're looking for a simulation where you are a hacker paid by big companies to take on big jobs against individuals and other companies, look to Uplink for that, especially with the UplinkOS GUI mod.

And then this is where I tell you "but if you're looking for...", cause it's hard to pin Hacknet's strength. Like I said, it has good setups for its missions, but the actual main plot is honestly kind of weak. So why do I still recommend it? I guess it's in the charm of it all quite frankly between the music, the flashy aesthetic, and all that.

Like honestly, the ONLY reason I actually finally got through the main plot of this game was because a video got recommended to me of the games last mission out of context, and everything on screen along with Carpenter Brut's "Roller Mobster" was enough to make me think "What's going on?" and play though the game just to see what was up. And honestly it was a bit underwhelming once it was all said and done, lol

So do I still recommend this game?

It's 10USD, and it often goes on sale for like less than 2USD, so I'd either way.

Is the DLC worth it? I actually think the last mission of the DLC is better as it gives a far better "emotion" to you the player as you're doing it, so totally consider picking it up if it's on sale.

Also it's absolute bullcrap I can't do "rm -rf /" or any such variation of such. I don't care if teaching newbs the most dangerous command might make them also do it to their own terminal on accident, that's their fault and mine if I'm not paying attention.

Seriously, it would have made the last mission just more hilarious to just do that, crack open a can of coke, and just watch and wait for everything to delete.

Yeah, what can I say, this is one of the most original games I've ever played.  Actually it might  be the most original.  Once you get the hang of this game, after the first couple missions where you're learning how the game works, it becomes one of the most immersive experiences out there.  With the music playing in your headphones, the lights out, and a beer on  your desk, if you let yourself get lost in it, it really feels like you're hacking into something that really exists.  You need to find that medical record and delete it, you need to find a way to decypher the encrypted programs.  It  is a lot of fun, and I played about 3 hours of this game, before I immediately bought the DLC for it.  I'm slowly playing through now, as I don't want it to end too quickly.  There are parts of the game I had to look up because I had no idea how to continue.  It doesn't hold your hand, it just gives you ways to solve the problem, and expects you to figure it out.  Find the file, use the  tools provided to extract it, and upload it to a communal server.  Simple right?  Not exactly.  Sometimes this game really picks your brain.  I am loving it, and if you think you might enjoy a mostly text based game about hacking, just buy it.  Buy it, and turn your RGB on, crack a cold beer, turn the lights out, and put your headphones on, and get lost.

Dreams are mysterious things. Some of us dream of lambs. Some of us dream of shoes. Others dream of being handed a mythical key to all computers that you can launch through a random terminal to remotely control PCs and brick it like a laid off labourer with poor aim. Others still dream of ketchup.

Hacknet hears your dreams, and fulfills exactly one of them.

You, the ingame you not the greasy pervert reading this, are the legendary, mythical, as the prophecy-foretold Script Kiddie, and you've been gifted the Ultimate Password Breaker that was left around when Uplink had its gateway seized. All you need is to open the ports, but don't worry you've been gifted someone else's programs to do that too. Largely at random. 
In retrospect, not the best prophecy. The one about landing a cool kickflip was better.

Yes, this is the spiritual sequel to Uplink. Instead of taking on completely randomized jobs you grind for upgrades, forever, because Uplink's progression was designed by a psychopath, you've got a branching set of missions, well paced, that range from "open all the ports and rifle around their belongings" to "open all the ports and rifle around their belongings on several systems".
There's even characters, and plot. Payoff. Most importantly, a terminal you can rapid fire commands in to do your bidding with the efficiency of a kalashnikov in a kindergarten.

FOR THE SMALL PRICE OF [&!=CURRENCY.x] YOU CAN VICARIOUSLY LIVE AS SOMEONE WHO KNOWS HOW COMMAND PROMPTS WORK.

The challenge in Hacknet is in mastering the interface. The puzzle is in remembering when to use your tools and getting past timed traces, the mechanical depth is in how fast you can fire off commands, the strategy is in prioritizing program order and managing your own filesystem, the masterful strategy is in alt-tabbing out of the rather sus website before your boss walks in. 

Honestly it's about as deep as a puddle. Messing with the pretend EZ Bake Oven terminal is just fun.

You're not doing much more than firing off command lines and navigating filesystems, but the game runs with that concept and wins a marathon.
And then the expansion takes it further, presumably overtaking Forrest Gump at some point. Got shin splints and is in long-term rehabilitation. Get well cards and flowers are expected.

Hacknet is absolutely worth your time. Open your ports and let it hack into your heart. So long as you remember to give it the tools first and don't accidentally wipe your own system. I didn't. I presume it would be bad to do that, so I will deny it at any opportunity.

This game had an amazing story, as well as engaging gameplay, and even at the end with everything all tied up, I'm still craving for more. It's got a learning curve and is not action pack or constantly intense, but it does have its intense moments. If your interested in the concept of hacking and cyber security then this game is a must play, who knows it may inspire you to learn even more.

This game is Loads better at "pretend hacker" than something like Uplink (which was more just clicking GUI interfaces that are complete fiction) Hacknet will at least teach you a *little* bit of Unix. Not much, there's one mission where it warns that "only unix vetrans should do this" and it's just a search/replace thing...

I wish they had ported over more bash functionality into the game, I'd love the ability to chain commands, add more robust logging (I kept expecting to find clues in logs, and it was NEVER the case) Lastly it would be nice if the world reacted to your hacks. The world is fairly static and other than emails telling you "good job!" you don't really get any feedback outside a couple scripted events. I'd love to see an in-world "news site" that would react to your hacks and maybe even start calling you out if you aren't careful enough covering your tracks (see hitman blood money's newspaper). Also it didn't really support "creative solutions" doing silly things like replacing 1's in a sys binary file with "p" and rebooting doesn't break systems or count as a mission complete in situations where it should.

In a sequel I'd love to see more Unix concepts explored, and have a more interactive world that reacts differently depending on how reckless/careful you are with your hacks. Some recommendations for commands i'd explore:

top
vim -alike
recursive commands
cron jobs
tail
less
&& chain commands
vpn tunnels & DNS addresses
MAC addresses
rolling back/reflashing firmware versions
port forwarding
cypher-based passwords
Plaintext passwords stored in program/cron job configs

and even more I'm probably forgetting.

also a really cool thing to have:
user-created hacking utilities (sharable in workshop for use in other missions)
